teaching.task: # HMS Year 11 V05 (The body and mind in motion): efficiency of the cardiovascular system. What makes one cardiovascular system more efficient than another, and what takes that efficiency away? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: Stroke volume is the blood the left ventricle pushes out per beat. Cardiac output is the blood moved per minute: heart rate times stroke volume. At rest, about seventy beats of seventy millilitres, roughly five litres. Endurance training enlarges the left ventricle's chamber, so each beat pushes out more. The runner's hundred and twenty millilitres a beat, times forty-two, makes about five litres. The untrained heart's sixty-six needs seventy-six beats. Same output, fewer beats. That's efficiency: the oxygen the body needs, at the lowest cost, with room to rise. So the low heart rate is a sign of fitness, not the cause. Delivery runs through three links. Link one, loading: oxygen crosses into the blood at the alveoli. Link two, carrying: haemoglobin holds about two hundred millilitres of oxygen in every litre of blood. Link three, delivering: the heart and vessels move that blood to the muscle. Five litres a minute times two hundred millilitres a litre gives the litre a minute on our readout. When a link weakens, the heart usually beats faster to keep delivery up. Delivery is saved, but each litre of oxygen costs more heartbeats. That's lost efficiency. Altitude starts with a trap. Mountain air is still about twenty-one per cent oxygen. What falls is air pressure, so the partial pressure of oxygen falls, from about a hundred and sixty to about a hundred and eighteen at two and a half thousand metres. The gradient at the alveoli shrinks, so less oxygen crosses, and each litre leaves the lungs carrying less. That's link one. Straight away you breathe harder, and your heart rate rises at every pace. Your V O two max, the most oxygen you can take in and use, falls too.

scenes.teachingReason: Stroke volume is the blood the left ventricle pushes out per beat. Cardiac output is the blood moved per minute: heart rate times stroke volume. At rest, about seventy beats of seventy millilitres, roughly five litres. Endurance training enlarges the left ventricle's chamber, so each beat pushes out more. The runner's hundred and twenty millilitres a beat, times forty-two, makes about five litres. The untrained heart's sixty-six needs seventy-six beats. Same output, fewer beats. That's efficiency: the oxygen the body needs, at the lowest cost, with room to rise. So the low heart rate is a sign of fitness, not the cause.

scenes.teachingReason: Delivery runs through three links. Link one, loading: oxygen crosses into the blood at the alveoli. Link two, carrying: haemoglobin holds about two hundred millilitres of oxygen in every litre of blood. Link three, delivering: the heart and vessels move that blood to the muscle. Five litres a minute times two hundred millilitres a litre gives the litre a minute on our readout. When a link weakens, the heart usually beats faster to keep delivery up. Delivery is saved, but each litre of oxygen costs more heartbeats. That's lost efficiency.

scenes.teachingReason: Altitude starts with a trap. Mountain air is still about twenty-one per cent oxygen. What falls is air pressure, so the partial pressure of oxygen falls, from about a hundred and sixty to about a hundred and eighteen at two and a half thousand metres. The gradient at the alveoli shrinks, so less oxygen crosses, and each litre leaves the lungs carrying less. That's link one. Straight away you breathe harder, and your heart rate rises at every pace. Your V O two max, the most oxygen you can take in and use, falls too.

scenes.teachingReason: Over two to four weeks, the body adapts. That's acclimatisation. The kidneys sense low oxygen and release a hormone, erythropoietin, or E P O, which makes more red blood cells. Haemoglobin rises, so each litre carries more again. The body repairs link one by strengthening link two, and muscles may grow more capillaries. That's why athletes live high and train low: they sleep at altitude for the adaptation, and come down to train at full intensity.

scenes.teachingReason: Link two is haemoglobin. Since ninety-eight per cent of oxygen rides on it, lose a fifth of your haemoglobin, and each litre carries a fifth less. Breathing harder can't fix that: there's nowhere to put the extra oxygen. So the heart has to move more litres, and heart rate is higher at every workload, most of all in exercise. That's anaemia: too little haemoglobin. The commonest cause is low iron, the atom that holds the oxygen. The risk is highest in teenage girls who menstruate, endurance athletes, and low-iron diets.

scenes.teachingReason: Link three can fail even with a good pump and good blood. In atherosclerosis, fatty plaque builds up in artery walls over decades. It narrows the channel, so less blood gets through, and stiffens the wall, so the artery can't widen to send more blood to working muscle. Where it happens decides the damage. In the coronary arteries, which supply the heart muscle, it causes chest pain on exertion, called angina, and a full blockage causes a heart attack. In the legs, walking hurts. In the brain, it can cause a stroke.

scenes.teachingReason: Stiff, narrow arteries also raise blood pressure, which sets a trap. The left ventricle must push harder, so its wall thickens. The runner's heart is bigger too. So ask what grew. In the runner, the chamber grew, so stroke volume rises. With high blood pressure, the wall grew, the chamber fills less easily, and stroke volume can't rise as much. Two big hearts: one efficient, one struggling.

scenes.teachingReason: Other factors fit the same chain. Endurance training strengthens link three: a bigger ventricle and more blood volume raise stroke volume. Dehydration shrinks the plasma, so stroke volume falls and heart rate drifts up through a long game. Heat sends blood to the skin, competing with muscle. Smoking hits all three links at once. Carbon monoxide grabs haemoglobin about two hundred times more tightly than oxygen, taking its seats, nicotine narrows vessels, and smoke damages the airways.

scenes.teachingReason: Start with the premise: still twenty-one per cent oxygen, but lower pressure, so a lower partial pressure. A smaller gradient means less oxygen loads. The classic mistake is opening with less oxygen in the air.

scenes.motionPurpose:
Heading on screen: "Key notes: what to write in your book".

1. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (about 5 L/min at rest).
2. Efficient: the oxygen needed at least cost; a low resting HR is a sign, not a cause.
3. Chain: load (alveoli), carry (haemoglobin), deliver (heart and vessels).
4. Altitude: still 21% oxygen, lower pressure; over weeks EPO raises red cells.
5. Anaemia weakens carrying; atherosclerosis narrows and stiffens arteries.

Memory card (the scene 11 card) beside the notes. Each bullet one line of at most 86 characters. Hold about 45 seconds in all.
